gist: In a July 31, 2026 no-guest episode, Kevin Muir and co-host Patrick argue that Fed chair Worsh's hawkish-talk-but-no-hike FOMC decision was a credibility mistake that pushed the 30-year yield through its May and October 2023 highs, and that a later 'panic hike' will be the policy error that tips the US into recession. They pair that with a post-mortem on the largest momentum-factor drawdown outside recessions, the Leopold/Situational Awareness 4x-leveraged blowup as a mechanical driver of the AI unwind, and a positioning tour (COT data) showing record yen shorts, five-year-high crude shorts, flatlined gold specs and crowded-but-unsqueezed long-bond shorts.

themes.theme: Worsh's hawkish hold and the bond-market credibility break

insights.claim: Going into the July 2026 FOMC, Fed funds futures priced roughly a 38-40% chance of a rate HIKE while only 4 of the 64 economists in Bloomberg's survey forecast one - the widest market-vs-economist split the hosts can recall for any Fed meeting.
insights.speaker: Kevin Muir
insights.so_what: When derivatives and forecasters diverge that far, the mispriced leg is the tradeable one; Goldman flagged that whatever happened would produce the largest front-end move of any recent meeting.
insights.quote: they surveyed 64 economists, only four had a hike forecast

insights.claim: The 38% hike probability was largely manufactured by hedging flow, not forecasting: a single massive persistent seller of the August Fed funds futures contract dominated the STIR market for the month after Worsh said the Fed would stop holding the market's hand.
insights.speaker: Kevin Muir
insights.so_what: CME-implied odds should be read as a funding-hedge print, not a consensus forecast, when one flow dominates the contract - it creates fadeable distortions.
insights.quote: There has been a massive seller in Fed funds futures for the the August contract, just massive.

insights.claim: Worsh's refusal to pre-commit forced levered players - especially pod shops running the long-cash-bond/short-future basis trade - to lock in funding via Fed funds futures because a surprise hike would blow up their carry, which is the mechanism that lifted implied hike odds.
insights.speaker: Kevin Muir
insights.so_what: Removing forward guidance imposes a real funding-hedge cost on the basis trade, so a less predictable Fed structurally widens front-end risk premia and can force basis-trade deleveraging.

insights.claim: Even for someone right that Worsh would not hike, buying stocks was the wrong expression because equities had already baked it in and barely moved on the announcement, whereas Fed funds futures repriced instantly - a clean arbitrage between the two markets' beliefs.
insights.speaker: Kevin Muir
insights.so_what: Trade a macro view in the instrument that has not already discounted it; check cross-asset implied odds before sizing an equity bet on a Fed outcome.
insights.quote: the correct trade was to go and buy Fed funds futures because they instantly repriced based upon them not raising rates

insights.claim: Muir was at 50/50 on a hike versus the market's 38%, on game-theory grounds: passing in both June and July with inflation still above target forces a more politically awkward move in September, close to the midterms.
insights.speaker: Kevin Muir
insights.so_what: Political-calendar constraints argue the Fed's optionality shrinks with every pass, skewing the front end toward a forced move rather than a smooth path.

insights.claim: Not hiking pushed long-end yields UP: the 30-year yield spiked during Worsh's press conference rather than on the statement, and on the daily chart cleared the important May 2026 high and the October 2023 high that had formed the third top of a 'triple top'.
insights.speaker: Patrick (co-host)
insights.so_what: A confirmed technical breakout in 30-year yields on a dovish-outcome day is the tell that the long end is trading credibility, not policy rate direction.
insights.quote: there's no such thing as a triple top

insights.claim: The episode is a live counterexample to the retail reflex that 'the Fed not tightening means buy bonds' - here the absence of a hike raised long rates because the market lost confidence the Fed was serious about the 2% target.
insights.speaker: Kevin Muir
insights.so_what: Position the curve, not the level: dovish surprises can steepen violently and lose money for duration longs when credibility is the binding constraint.
insights.quote: him not tightening actually caused rates to rise

insights.claim: Worsh re-committed explicitly to getting inflation back to 2% at this press conference while simultaneously pausing with employment fine and inflation above target - the contradiction, plus circular answers and questions-answered-with-questions, is what lost the bond market.
insights.speaker: Kevin Muir
insights.so_what: Watch the gap between stated reaction function and delivered action; that gap, not the level of rates, is what repriced the long end.
insights.quote: you can't say you're going to get to 2% and then not do anything about it

insights.claim: Muir rejects the widespread 'Worsh is Trump's puppet' view on term-length grounds - Worsh has a seven-year term versus roughly two years left for Trump - and thinks Worsh is protecting his legacy past the administration.
insights.speaker: Kevin Muir
insights.so_what: If Fed independence is real, the market's implicit assumption that hikes are politically impossible is mispriced - and cheaply expressed in Fed funds futures.
insights.quote: Wars is there for seven years. Trump is there for two.

insights.claim: Muir's central sequence: Worsh eventually hikes, but as a bond-market-forced panic hike that is far worse than a pre-emptive one, which becomes the policy error that tips the economy into recession and ultimately produces much lower rates - the point to buy the long end.
insights.speaker: Kevin Muir
insights.so_what: Sequencing matters for duration: stay short/absent the long end through the panic-hike phase, then buy it once the recession is being priced.
insights.quote: I think that he will raise rates and it'll be a mistake in that he's made it so that the pressure will be it'll be a panic raise which will be way worse than a than a raise where you're getting out ahead of it.

insights.claim: The dangerous regime the hosts are watching is a return of the tariff-episode pattern where stocks, bonds AND the US dollar fall together - which they say is exactly what the last few days look like, raising the risk of the long end going no bid.
insights.speaker: Kevin Muir
insights.so_what: The triple-down correlation is the signature of a funding/credibility shock rather than a growth scare, and it breaks the 60/40 hedge.

insights.claim: Worsh has created five committees despite hating bureaucracy, and Muir's causal chain runs from a more confused market to higher volatility to a higher risk premium to lower financial asset prices.
insights.speaker: Kevin Muir
insights.so_what: Policy opacity is a valuation input: it argues for structurally cheaper multiples and for owning volatility rather than carry.
insights.quote: if you make the market more confused, you have more volatility. And if you have more volatility, that means that the risk premium should go up.

themes.theme: Front-end pricing, one-and-done, and the policy-error trade

insights.claim: After the hold, the market prices roughly 67% odds of a September hike, about a 20% chance of a second hike by October, and a December distribution split 40% for one hike versus 37% for two.
insights.speaker: Patrick (co-host)
insights.so_what: Roughly one-and-a-half hikes are already in the price, which caps the payoff to further hawkish surprises in the front end.

insights.claim: December 2026 SOFR futures trade at 95.92 versus December 2027 at 95.86 - about five to six basis points apart - meaning STIR traders are pricing essentially no directional move in rates through all of 2027.
insights.speaker: Patrick (co-host)
insights.so_what: A flat 2026-2027 SOFR strip is a cheap option on directional conviction returning; any resolution toward cuts or hikes reprices the 2027 tenor hardest.
insights.quote: the December 2026 sofur is trending at 9592 and the December 2027 is a 95.86. Literally five basis points different.

insights.claim: Both hosts agree with 100% conviction that the short end - SOFR and the two-year - is now pricing close to the top of the interest-rate cycle, giving asymmetric payoff to being long the short end even while the long bond remains risky.
insights.speaker: Kevin Muir
insights.so_what: Curve trade: own the front end for the recession/cut optionality while avoiding or shorting the long end that carries the credibility risk.

insights.claim: Muir's actual position is a December SOFR one-by-two put ratio spread - buying one put and selling two further out-of-the-money puts - explicitly structured because he thinks the Fed hikes once, not on a three-hike campaign.
insights.speaker: Kevin Muir
insights.so_what: A concrete, cheap structure for the one-and-done view: it pays on a hawkish repricing but caps out where a hiking campaign would be priced.

insights.claim: Muir directly contests the widely held rule that the Fed never hikes only once - Bank of America at one point forecast three hikes (September, October, December) - arguing the Fed could hike once, see things roll over fast, and be cutting shockingly quickly.
insights.speaker: Kevin Muir
insights.so_what: If the hiking cycle is one-and-done, selling further OTM front-end puts (or fading multi-hike forecasts) is the edge.
insights.quote: there have been so many things that have never happened before that are happening now that you should be very careful about using old playbooks

insights.claim: Patrick's policy-error case rests on the source of inflation being a war-driven supply shock - disrupted oil logistics and fertilizer shortages - which a monetary tool cannot fix, so hiking just adds a second drag onto an economy already taxed by the war.
insights.speaker: Patrick (co-host)
insights.so_what: Supply-driven inflation means rate hikes buy disinflation only via demand destruction, raising the odds the terminal outcome is recession plus rapid cuts.

insights.claim: The 'triple whammy' recession framework: the war acting as a global tax, Fed tightening into that, and an AI-bubble-driven equity drawdown as the third input, together producing economic data that can no longer justify higher rates.
insights.speaker: Patrick (co-host)
insights.so_what: A useful checklist for the recession trade - watch whether the AI drawdown persists, because it is the marginal third input that flips the outcome.

insights.claim: Only about 2% of respondents in the Bank of America fund manager survey are calling for a hard landing, versus 2023 when everyone expected one and it did not arrive - which Muir reads as evidence recession is far closer than consensus believes.
insights.speaker: Kevin Muir
entities: Bank of America fund manager survey
insights.so_what: Recession hedges are cheap when 98% of allocators do not want them; the mirror-image of 2023 argues for owning front-end receivers and equity downside.
insights.quote: I think we're way closer to a recession than anyone believes.

insights.claim: Inverting their own base case Munger-style, the bear case for bonds is that the AI drawdown is an SVB-style hiccup that washes out and resumes, private money-supply expansion continues, fiscal cuts arrive before the midterms, and rates head toward 8%.
insights.speaker: Kevin Muir
insights.so_what: Defines the stop-loss for the recession trade: resumed credit expansion plus fiscal easing is the falsifier, and it implies a violent long-end selloff rather than a rally.

insights.claim: There is roughly $100 trillion of total debt in the US system - the entire credit stock, not just government debt - carrying about $7 trillion a year in gross interest, so the economy cannot tolerate the rate levels it withstood when debt per capita and deficits were far smaller.
insights.speaker: Kevin Muir
insights.so_what: Debt stock caps the terminal rate: the 'rates were higher before so they can be again' argument ignores that the interest burden is now systemically binding.

themes.theme: The AI/momentum unwind and the 2000 NASDAQ analog

insights.claim: The momentum volatility factor just posted its highest one-month realized volatility on record outside recessions, with the only comparable episodes being the GFC and 2020 - and it was one of the largest one-month drawdowns for momentum hedge funds in a decade.
insights.speaker: Kevin Muir
insights.so_what: A factor-vol print at GFC/COVID levels means risk models will force further de-grossing regardless of fundamentals, extending the unwind.
insights.quote: the momentum volatility factor had the highest realized v over one u month apart from recessions that we've ever seen

insights.claim: The index the hosts call 'the Cosby' - the memory/semiconductor epicenter of the AI trade - fell 44% peak to trough at the lows and traced an Eiffel Tower pattern, wiping out weeks of gains in three to four weeks.
insights.speaker: Kevin Muir
insights.so_what: A 44% drawdown in the leadership index with the S&P barely down flags the unwind as positioning-driven and not yet transmitted to the broad market.

insights.claim: The convexity trap in bounce math: an almost 18% up-day in the AI/memory complex did not retrace half the 40%-plus decline - it only returned price to Monday's level, and did not even close above it.
insights.speaker: Patrick (co-host)
insights.so_what: Percentage symmetry is an illusion after big drawdowns; do not read violent rallies as evidence the damage has been repaired.
insights.quote: You lost 43%, but then you made 43%. But doesn't mean you're back to the highs. It means you're halfway to the highs.

insights.claim: Patrick's preferred template is the NASDAQ in 2000 - roughly a 400% two-year run, a 40% peak-to-trough drop, then a 43% three-month rally that never approached the prior high before rolling over and dying - which he says maps onto the current memory/semi complex better than the silver analog.
insights.speaker: Patrick (co-host)
insights.so_what: Gives a concrete roadmap: expect a multi-month powerful rally that fails well below the highs, i.e. sell strength rather than buy the dip.
insights.quote: the largest and sharpest and most vicious rallies occur within bare markets

insights.claim: Against a famous strategist arguing you should close your eyes and buy tech including in 2000, Muir notes a 2000 index buyer did not break even even nominally until around 2015, and that assumes you owned the index rather than individual names where roughly 90% were wiped out.
insights.speaker: Kevin Muir
insights.so_what: Post-bubble recovery time, not just drawdown depth, is the risk - a reason to avoid single-name AI bets even if you believe in the technology.
insights.quote: if you had bought in 2000, you weren't even on a nominal basis till like 2015

insights.claim: Muir expects semiconductors and memory stocks to trace silver's post-bubble path: sharp correction, large corrective rally, then a persistent drift lower rather than a V-shaped recovery.
insights.speaker: Kevin Muir
insights.so_what: The drift-lower path punishes both dip buyers and impatient shorts; it favours selling rallies and owning long-dated downside rather than chasing.

insights.claim: Muir insists valuation was the dismissed variable that enabled this bubble - it can be ignored over the short run because multiples can keep expanding, but it determines everything over the long run.
insights.speaker: Kevin Muir
insights.so_what: A reminder to underwrite AI exposure on entry multiple, since the long-run return is set there regardless of the technology's transformational status.
insights.quote: Nothing matters more than valuation.

themes.theme: Leopold's Situational Awareness blowup and levered-ETF mechanics

insights.claim: The Situational Awareness fund run by Leopold - a 24-year-old ex-OpenAI author - was four-times levered in one of the most volatile sectors in the world, at one point running roughly $40 billion of fund equity against about $60 billion of exposure, which cannot be done on traditional margin.
insights.speaker: Patrick (co-host)
insights.so_what: Leverage of that size can only be run through ISDA/swap lines, which is precisely what made the fund's positions visible and stoppable.
insights.quote: he was situationally aware of AI but not situationally aware of how stock markets work

insights.claim: Trading via ISDA accounts and swaps means too many counterparties know your position, which turns a large levered book into a target - the same mechanism that killed Amaranth's natural gas Widowmaker spread and squeezed Bill Ackman's public Herbalife short via Icahn.
insights.speaker: Kevin Muir
insights.so_what: Position visibility is a first-order risk for anyone running size in illiquid or crowded exposures - and creates a repeatable predatory trade for those on the other side.
insights.quote: Wall Street is like they eat their young.

insights.claim: The Long-Term Capital lesson from When Genius Failed applies directly: once the street knows they can take you down 50%, the fundamentals of your book are irrelevant because they can take you the whole way.
insights.speaker: Kevin Muir
insights.so_what: Drawdown, not thesis quality, determines survival in levered structures - a reason to size for the mark-to-market path, not the terminal value.
insights.quote: Once they realize that they can take you down 50%, they realize they can take you down the whole way.

insights.claim: Muir attributes a meaningful part of the last one to two weeks of the AI correction to Leopold being stopped out and prime brokers liquidating his book, and argues the subsequent bounce reflects the selling STOPPING rather than new demand appearing.
insights.speaker: Kevin Muir
insights.so_what: A supply-exhaustion bounce is not a demand signal; without the levered marginal buyer, rallies should stall - a setup to sell rather than chase.
insights.quote: To me it's more that the the selling stopped and that was the important part.

insights.claim: Leopold reportedly also held short positions in Adobe and other software names, and semis/memory traded almost tick-for-tick inverse to software - a shockingly negative correlation that identifies the long/short pair being unwound under the surface.
insights.speaker: Patrick (co-host)
insights.so_what: The semis-vs-software negative correlation is a real-time tracker of hedge-fund de-grossing; when it normalizes, the forced unwind is finished.

insights.claim: Two- and three-times levered ETFs have never been larger, and their end-of-day rebalancing mechanically buys more as prices rise and sells more as they fall - a flow that flattered the AI rally and then amplified the crash.
insights.speaker: Kevin Muir
insights.so_what: Record levered-ETF assets are a measurable pro-cyclical flow; their size sets the size of forced end-of-day selling in a drawdown.

insights.claim: The 3x semiconductor ETF fell from roughly $300 to $100 in a month - about a 70% drawdown - clearing below its June and May lows and trading back to February/March prices, while the unlevered SMH barely closed below its May low even once.
insights.speaker: Patrick (co-host)
insights.so_what: Quantifies the volatility-decay and daily-rebalance slippage penalty: the levered vehicle gave back a year of gains on a move the underlying barely registered technically.

insights.claim: Muir's forward conclusion from the blowup is structural: nobody will extend three or four times leverage on these names again and retail will not double down at the top, so it will be tough for the AI leadership complex to perform going forward.
insights.speaker: Kevin Muir
insights.so_what: The marginal levered buyer is gone, which caps upside even if fundamentals hold - a case for structurally lower multiples in the leaders.

themes.theme: S&P resilience, Mag 7 dispersion and the staples-versus-momentum question

insights.claim: Despite the leadership being destroyed - Leopold stopped out, Micron and the semiconductors nailed - the S&P 500 is only about 3% from its highs, which Muir calls astounding and attributes to sector rotation rather than liquidity contagion.
insights.speaker: Kevin Muir
insights.so_what: Index-level calm masks a violent internal rotation; hedging via the index has been ineffective while single-factor exposure was the real risk.

insights.claim: Market breadth measured by the number of stocks trending reached 72-73% a few days ago - a fresh high not seen since January - and the equal-weight index made a fresh high on Wednesday, confirming the money leaving semis was sprinkled everywhere else.
insights.speaker: Patrick (co-host)
insights.so_what: Broadening breadth during a leadership crash is the rotation signature; if breadth rolls over while leaders stay weak, that is the confirmation the whole market is turning.

insights.claim: Per Goldman Sachs' CTA work, the 7450-7400 area on the S&P is the first layer of short-term CTA sell triggers; the market briefly poked through it and recovered, so CTAs are now a live marginal seller that bulls must keep the index elevated to avoid activating.
insights.speaker: Patrick (co-host)
insights.so_what: A concrete level to watch: sustained trade below 7400 turns systematic flow from neutral to a mechanical seller of the index.

insights.claim: Muir concedes Mag 7 valuations are not bubble-like on earnings - though the earnings quality is arguable - but insists their price path is what matters because roughly one third of the index sits in those seven stocks.
insights.speaker: Kevin Muir
insights.so_what: The Mag 7 not selling off alongside memory and the semis index is the sole reason the index has held; their break is the trigger for index-level damage.

insights.claim: Within the Mag 7 the dispersion is wide: Google gapped down on disappointing results but is being bought on the dip and saving the day, Tesla and Meta are weak with Meta holding its prior low, Apple gapped below its 50-day yet absorbed heavy flows from sellers of semis, and Microsoft joining marked a turnaround in software broadly.
insights.speaker: Patrick (co-host)
insights.so_what: The semis-to-software/Apple rotation is where the money actually went - a pair to monitor for when the rotation exhausts and index support fails.

insights.claim: Even with breadth and equal-weight at highs, Muir believes the rotation is late-stage and the whole market rolls over soon, because the small non-consensus names are too small to offset selling in what everyone owns for long.
insights.speaker: Kevin Muir
insights.so_what: Treat broadening breadth as a temporary shock absorber, not an all-clear; the index-level move comes when rotation capacity is exhausted.
insights.quote: I think we're getting close to the end of this that that the the whole market's going to roll over soon.

insights.claim: Patrick speculates Steve Eisman's CNBC appearance - selling Google, going to cash and dismissing staples - captures the consensus that staples are a value trap, and may mark the capitulation low in the value-versus-momentum factor, citing General Mills falling from $90 to $30 and Clorox and Whirlpool as charts of death.
insights.speaker: Patrick (co-host)
insights.so_what: A named consensus view on tape is a sentiment marker: if performance appears in staples, performance-chasers rotate there, making beaten-down staples an asymmetric contrarian long.
insights.quote: what am I going to do buy a Clorox? That never goes up.

themes.theme: Yen intervention, GPIF reallocation and the carry-trade fourth shoe

insights.claim: The Bank of Japan confirmed - not rumoured - intervention and Muir believes it was the largest intervention it has ever done, yet the yen only returned to its May levels after having been at lows for the current move days earlier.
insights.speaker: Kevin Muir
insights.so_what: Record intervention buying only a two-month retracement is a weak result - historically each intervention has been another opportunity to sell the yen, not a trend change.

insights.claim: The asymmetry of intervention: weakening your own currency is easy because you can print unlimited amounts of it, while strengthening it is much harder because you eventually run out of foreign currency to sell.
insights.speaker: Kevin Muir
insights.so_what: Explains why yen-strengthening interventions have finite ammunition and why the durable fix has to be flow-based, not reserve-based.
insights.quote: intervening to get your currency down is actually pretty easy because you have the ability to produce unlimited amounts of your currency.

insights.claim: Muir's core yen thesis is that the durable fix is reallocating Japanese savings: GPIF, the largest pension plan in the world, currently runs 25% foreign bonds, 25% foreign stocks, 25% local stocks and 25% local bonds after the Abenomics-era shift away from roughly 75% domestic, and Japan's finance minister fired a shot across the bow a couple of weeks ago signalling a change is coming.
insights.speaker: Kevin Muir
insights.so_what: A GPIF mandate change is the identifiable catalyst that converts the yen from a carry funding currency into a multi-year bid - and it is a policy announcement you can wait for.
insights.quote: once that actual policy change occurs in the GPIF that is going to mean that the US JPY is going to be on offer forever, meaning that the yen will be bid for years and years and years to come.

insights.claim: Commitment of Traders data as of the 21st show large specs net short about 260,000 yen futures contracts - the largest net short in at least five years - with the positioning score at the 1st percentile on a one-year lookback and near five-year lows as a percentage of open interest, while net longs have stayed flat.
insights.speaker: Patrick (co-host)
insights.so_what: Record one-sided shorts with no offsetting longs means any trend break forces trend-followers to unwind, creating outsized short-squeeze potential in the yen.

insights.claim: Both hosts treat a yen carry-trade unwind as a distinct fourth headwind for risk assets - on top of the war tax, Fed tightening and the AI drawdown - that could push risk assets offered.
insights.speaker: Kevin Muir
insights.so_what: Yen strength is the cross-asset transmission channel to watch: it converts a factor unwind into a global deleveraging event.

insights.claim: CHF/JPY is Muir's preferred FX proxy for the US stock market because Swiss institutions run high hedge ratios - selling more dollars for francs as their US equity holdings rise - while Japanese investors, especially through retail NISA accounts, buy US equities unhedged; a US equity decline therefore forces Japanese repatriation into yen and Swiss hedge unwinds out of francs.
insights.speaker: Kevin Muir
insights.so_what: A single FX cross that expresses the equity-drawdown thesis with cleaner carry and liquidity than equity puts - and Patrick notes it has just broken down through a year-long range to lower lows.

themes.theme: Commodity and Treasury positioning: crude shorts, PBoC gold, copper, uranium

insights.claim: Crude oil rallied roughly 40% off the low made when the attempted peace deal was announced, reclaiming and consolidating above its 50-day moving average with prices back at $85-86, even though the initial selloff had ignored depleted inventories entirely.
insights.speaker: Patrick (co-host)
insights.so_what: Oil rebuilding above its 50-day while war uncertainty persists and inventories are depleted sets up a bullish base - and the 40% rally still leaves it far below the highs.

insights.claim: Crude COT data as of the 21st show gross short positioning at a five-year high, net positioning as a percentage of open interest lower only before the war started, and no short covering through the 40% rally, while longs were squeezed from about 390,000 contracts in late May down to about 300,000 without rebuilding.
insights.speaker: Patrick (co-host)
insights.so_what: Record shorts that have not been shaken out plus absent longs is the most asymmetric setup discussed on the show - upside in crude is squeeze-fuelled.
insights.quote: we have not seen this many people short oil in the futures market on this these contracts at any point in the last 5 years

insights.claim: Muir argues that persistently talking the oil price down destroys the natural supply of sellers at higher prices, so if something genuinely bad happens there is nobody offering at $120 and shorts must buy back - a policy-manufactured right-tail risk.
insights.speaker: Kevin Muir
insights.so_what: Suppressed prices with no natural sellers means upside gaps rather than orderly rallies - cheap out-of-the-money crude calls are the expression.
insights.quote: you've exposed us to this right tail risk that is much much higher because you've been so busy trying to talk the oil price down

insights.claim: Large-spec COT positioning in gold has barely budged all year - both long and short contract counts essentially flatlined through a bubble peak and a subsequent 25%-plus correction - meaning Western speculators are not driving the gold market.
insights.speaker: Patrick (co-host)
insights.so_what: If futures specs are absent, gold's marginal price setter is physical official-sector demand, which changes which indicators are actually predictive.

insights.claim: Muir argues gold is driven by the People's Bank of China - which just announced its largest monthly gold purchase ever - and that anyone using the US dollar and real rates to trade gold is using metrics that no longer matter, with the Trump election-sabotage accusations giving China more reason to buy gold instead of Treasuries.
insights.speaker: Kevin Muir
insights.so_what: Reframes the gold process variable entirely: track PBoC reserve announcements and US-China geopolitical friction rather than real yields.
insights.quote: this is further proof my theory that we aren't driving this bus. This bus has been driven by the people's bank of China

insights.claim: Patrick's gold plan is to wait for one more leg down driven by sympathy selling in a broad liquidity event - buying a flush to roughly $3,600-3,800 against an estimated $4,000 fair-value zone - and only if the weakness is accompanied by cross-asset selling rather than gold alone.
insights.speaker: Patrick (co-host)
insights.so_what: Gives a specific buy zone and a specific condition (intermarket selling, not idiosyncratic gold weakness) for adding gold exposure.

insights.claim: Treasury COT positioning is bifurcated: large specs sit at the 100th percentile in two-year notes but almost the zero percentile in long bonds, and crucially the two-year crowding came from huge short COVERING rather than new longs, while long-bond shorts keep building and keep being rewarded.
insights.speaker: Patrick (co-host)
insights.so_what: A crowded reading built on short covering is not a squeeze setup, so Patrick would not fade the two-year long - while the long-bond short is crowded but not yet squeezed.

insights.claim: Muir's caveat on all COT analysis is that the basis trade sits inside the reports - positions labelled speculative are often hedged - which makes the data more deceptive than it appears even if the story remains useful.
insights.speaker: Kevin Muir
insights.so_what: A necessary discount on Treasury COT signals: apparent spec shorts may be hedges, so squeeze inferences from the reports are less reliable in rates than in commodities.

insights.claim: Copper stands out from a commodity complex that has been hammered: it is holding 52-week and all-time highs with crowded but rewarded long large-spec positioning, and Muir sees 7.00-7.25 if it breaks out.
insights.speaker: Kevin Muir
insights.so_what: A confirmed breakout in copper would validate the crowded long and gives a defined target; failure at all-time highs with crowded longs is the risk case.
insights.quote: Copper is remaining at 52- week highs, actually all-time highs.

insights.claim: The physical uranium market has gone completely silent - flatlined like a hospital pulse monitor - and Cameco just reported a surprise loss, with the stock gapping higher and giving it all back, leaving uranium in a distribution cycle with no evidence of a new bull phase.
insights.speaker: Patrick (co-host)
insights.so_what: A failed earnings gap plus a dead physical market says respect the distribution phase in uranium regardless of the long-term nuclear story.
insights.quote: There is zero sign at this moment that either of these two markets have woken up.

insights.claim: Bitcoin could not even reach its 38% retracement on the bounce and now faces all of its prior trading ranges as overhead resistance, making another break lower the path of least resistance.
insights.speaker: Patrick (co-host)
insights.so_what: Failure to reclaim even a shallow retracement is a bearish tell; Bitcoin weakness alongside the AI unwind reinforces the broad risk-appetite drain thesis.
